claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of CT scans from 6 Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J).

claims.claim: The severity of skeletal defects is associated with the variability of soft palate clefts in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Notably, in analyzing the CT scans, we found that three out of six Runx2 mutant mice with missing palatine bones and more severe pterygoid plate defects also had soft palate clefts, while the other three Runx2 mutants without clefts exhibited palatine bones that were smaller, though not statistically significantly so, and less severe pterygoid plate defects, particularly shorter pterygoid plate height (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J), suggesting the severity of skeletal defects is associated with the variability of soft palate clefts in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between skeletal defect severity and cleft palate penetrance in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J).

claims.claim: The height of pterygoid plate was reduced in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Consistent with the CT scans, histological analysis showed that the height of pterygoid plate was reduced and muscle attachment was abnormal in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3G–H,L–M).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing reduced pterygoid plate height (Figure 3G-H, L-M).

claims.claim: Muscle attachment was abnormal in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Consistent with the CT scans, histological analysis showed that the height of pterygoid plate was reduced and muscle attachment was abnormal in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3G–H,L–M).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing abnormal muscle attachment (Figure 3G-H, L-M).

claims.claim: The tendon tissue did not extend to the midline in the palate primordium in the TVP region in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E16.5.
claims.source: Because the aponeurosis serves the important function of attaching the hard tissue to the muscle, we also analyzed the fibrous tendon tissue marked by Scx by RNAscope in situ hybridization. The tendon tissue did not extend to the midline in the palate primordium in the TVP region in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice as it did in the controls at E16.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3I–L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing altered Scx expression pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 3I-L).

claims.claim: The aponeurosis in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice was thinner and did not stretch from the lateral-oral side to the medial-nasal side at P0.
claims.source: It could be seen more clearly at P0 that the aponeurosis in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice was thinner and it did not stretch from the lateral-oral side to the medial-nasal side as it did in control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting its attachment to the posterior bone probably was likely abnormal.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing altered aponeurosis structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-D).

claims.claim: The muscle attachment defect of the TVP might be due to disruption of the hard tissue and aponeurosis.
claims.source: As Runx2 is not expressed in the perimysial site of the TVP region, Therefore, this muscle attachment defect of the TVP might be due to disruption of the hard tissue and aponeurosis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Runx2 expression in the TVP perimysial site and the observed defects in hard tissue and aponeurosis (Figure 2N-P, Figure 3—figure supplement 3I-L, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-D).

claims.claim: The muscles were reduced in size in the LVP region in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls.
claims.source: In the LVP region, the muscles were reduced in size in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls (Figure 3I–K,N–P).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing reduced muscle size (Figure 3I-K, N-P).

claims.claim: A significant number of LVP muscle fibers had anterior-posterior alignment in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, compared to the uniform lateral-medial alignment of LVP muscle fibers in controls.
claims.source: Interestingly, a significant number of LVP muscle fibers had anterior-posterior alignment in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3O–P), compared to the uniform lateral-medial alignment of LVP muscle fibers in controls (Figure 3J–K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing misoriented muscle fibers (Figure 3J-K, O-P).

claims.claim: The muscle fibers were mis-oriented in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, similar to the phenotype seen in patients with cleft soft palate.
claims.source: Interestingly, a significant number of LVP muscle fibers had anterior-posterior alignment in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3O–P), compared to the uniform lateral-medial alignment of LVP muscle fibers in controls (Figure 3J–K). This suggests that the muscle fibers were mis-oriented, similar to the phenotype seen in patients with cleft soft palate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of muscle fiber orientation in mutant mice to the known phenotype in cleft palate patients (Figure 3J-K, O-P).

claims.claim: The muscle fibers had centralized nuclei in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which suggests that they had muscle differentiation defects.
claims.source: Additionally, we observed that the muscle fibers had centralized nuclei in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which suggests that they had muscle differentiation defects (Figure 3P).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing centralized nuclei in muscle fibers (Figure 3P).

claims.claim: Similar muscle defects were also observed in other palatal muscles such as the PLP.
claims.source: Similar muscle defects were also observed in other palatal muscles such as the PLP (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–D,G–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing muscle defects in the PLP region (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-D, G-H).

claims.claim: Loss of Runx2 leads directly to defects in CNC-derived cells and indirectly to muscle defects in the soft palate.
claims.source: We concluded that loss of Runx2 leads directly to defects in CNC-derived cells and indirectly to muscle defects in the soft palate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed defects in CNC-derived tissues and muscles in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3).

claims.claim: There was no apparent change of early myogenic marker MyoD expression between control and Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E13.5 in the LVP.
claims.source: In the LVP, there was no apparent change of early myogenic marker MyoD expression between control and Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing similar MyoD expression at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).

claims.claim: MyoD staining revealed that defects started to appear at E14.5 in the LVP.
claims.source: MyoD staining revealed that defects started to appear at E14.5 (Figure 4A–B), when the palatal shelves began to grow and protrude towards the midline.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing altered MyoD expression at E14.5 (Figure 4A-B).

claims.claim: Expression of the late myogenic marker MHC was decreased in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E15.5.
claims.source: Expression of the late myogenic marker MHC was decreased in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E15.5 (Figure 4C–D), suggesting delayed muscle differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing reduced MHC expression at E15.5 (Figure 4C-D).

claims.claim: The reduced expression of MHC suggests delayed muscle differentiation in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Expression of the late myogenic marker MHC was decreased in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E15.5 (Figure 4C–D), suggesting delayed muscle differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reduced expression of the late myogenic marker MHC (Figure 4C-D).

claims.claim: The reduced expression of MHC persisted in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E16.5.
claims.source: This reduced expression of MHC persisted in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E16.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing continued reduced MHC expression at E16.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).

claims.claim: More immature myoblasts and fewer differentiated myofibers were present in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E15.5.
claims.source: MHC staining suggested that the myoblasts had fused to form myofibers, which were uniformly aligned in layers running in the lateral-to-medial direction in the LVP of control samples at E15.5 (Figure 4C). However, more immature myoblasts and fewer differentiated myofibers were present in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 4D) and the myofibers extended in different directions, potentially hindering further muscle development and compromising physiological function.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by MHC immunofluorescence staining showing altered muscle differentiation (Figure 4C-D).

claims.claim: The myofibers extended in different directions in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, potentially hindering further muscle development and compromising physiological function.
claims.source: MHC staining suggested that the myoblasts had fused to form myofibers, which were uniformly aligned in layers running in the lateral-to-medial direction in the LVP of control samples at E15.5 (Figure 4C). However, more immature myoblasts and fewer differentiated myofibers were present in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 4D) and the myofibers extended in different directions, potentially hindering further muscle development and compromising physiological function.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by MHC immunofluorescence staining showing misoriented myofibers (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: The proliferation rate of MyoD- CNC-derived cells did not have significant difference in the perimysial sites of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E14.5 and E15.5.
claims.source: In the LVP region at E14.5 and E15.5, the proliferation rate of MyoD- CNC-derived cells did not have significant difference in the perimysial sites of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls (Figure 4E–H,I,K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay showing no significant difference in CNC-derived cell proliferation (Figure 4E-H, I, K).

claims.claim: The proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was not significantly different between controls and Runx2 mutants at E14.5.
claims.source: The proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was not significantly different between controls and Runx2 mutants at E14.5 (Figure 4E–F,J), but a significant reduction in the proliferation rate was observed in Runx2 mutants at E15.5 (Figure 4G–H,L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay showing no significant difference in myogenic cell proliferation at E14.5 (Figure 4E-F, J).

claims.claim: A significant reduction in the proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was observed in Runx2 mutants at E15.5.
claims.source: The proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was not significantly different between controls and Runx2 mutants at E14.5 (Figure 4E–F,J), but a significant reduction in the proliferation rate was observed in Runx2 mutants at E15.5 (Figure 4G–H,L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay showing significantly reduced myogenic cell proliferation at E15.5 (Figure 4G-H, L).

claims.claim: The number of apoptotic cells was indistinguishable between controls and mutants at E14.5 and E15.5.
claims.source: We also performed caspase3 immunofluorescence staining to investigate cell apoptosis. The number of apoptotic cells was indistinguishable between controls and mutants at E14.5 and E15.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by caspase3 immunofluorescence staining showing no significant difference in apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H).

claims.claim: Altered signaling in CNC-derived cells might cause the reduction of MyoD expression as well as proliferation defects of myogenic cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: It is worth noting that although the proliferation rate of CNC-derived cells in the Runx2 mutant mice were not significantly different from that of the controls, we observed that they had fewer and less proliferative MyoD+ cells than Runx2fl/fl control mice. These differences might be due to altered signaling in CNC-derived cells causing the reduction of MyoD expression as well as proliferation defects of myogenic cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in MyoD+ cells and their proliferation despite normal CNC-derived cell proliferation (Figure 4E-H, I-L).

claims.claim: The composition of the CNC-derived cells was altered in the Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5.
claims.source: Using integration analysis based on shared variance, we identified similar cell clusters in the soft palates of control and Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at this stage. However, the composition of the CNC-derived cells was altered in the Runx2 mutants compared to controls (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by integration analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data showing altered cell cluster composition (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: The percentage of perimysial cells (Cluster 4) in the population decreased in Runx2 mutants.
claims.source: Using markers of different subtypes of CNC-derived cells, we observed that the percentage of perimysial cells (Cluster 4) in the population decreased in Runx2 mutants, while the percentage of midline mesenchymal cells (Clusters 0 and 3) increased (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the bar graph comparing cell percentages between control and mutant (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: The percentage of midline mesenchymal cells (Clusters 0 and 3) increased in Runx2 mutants.
claims.source: Using markers of different subtypes of CNC-derived cells, we observed that the percentage of perimysial cells (Cluster 4) in the population decreased in Runx2 mutants, while the percentage of midline mesenchymal cells (Clusters 0 and 3) increased (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the bar graph comparing cell percentages between control and mutant (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: In situ RNAscope staining revealed decreased expression of perimysial markers in the soft palates of Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5.
claims.source: Moreover, in situ RNAscope staining revealed decreased expression of perimysial markers in the soft palates of Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5, suggesting the CNC-derived perimysial populations were affected, potentially leading to further myogenic defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing reduced expression of Hic1 and Aldh1a2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-H).

claims.claim: The CNC-derived perimysial populations were affected in Runx2 mutants, potentially leading to further myogenic defects.
claims.source: Moreover, in situ RNAscope staining revealed decreased expression of perimysial markers in the soft palates of Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5, suggesting the CNC-derived perimysial populations were affected, potentially leading to further myogenic defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the decreased expression of perimysial markers and the known role of perimysial cells in muscle development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-H).

claims.claim: Bulk RNA-seq identified that certain genes associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells were differentially expressed in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Consistent with the scRNA-seq results, bulk RNA-seq also identified that certain genes associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells were differentially expressed in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq analysis showing differential gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claims.claim: A number of genes not exclusively associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells, including Twist1 and Meox2, were also identified as being differentially expressed in the bulk RNA-seq analysis.
claims.source: A number of genes not exclusively associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells, including Twist1 and Meox2, were also identified as being differentially expressed in the bulk RNA-seq analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq analysis showing differential expression of Twist1 and Meox2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claims.claim: Twist1 inhibits binding of Runx2 to its downstream targets and antagonizes Runx2's function in osteoblasts.
claims.source: We focused our attention on Twist1, which inhibits binding of Runx2 to its downstream targets and antagonizes Runx2's function in osteoblasts (Bialek et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies showing the antagonistic interaction between Twist1 and Runx2 (Bialek et al., 2004).

claims.claim: Twist1 is primarily expressed in midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+), while its expression in CNC-derived common progenitors and perimysial cells (Tfap2b+; Aldh1a2+) is relatively low.
claims.source: Based on the integration analysis of E13.5-E15.5 single-cell transcriptomes from controls, we observed Twist1 was primarily expressed in midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+), while its expression in CNC-derived common progenitors and perimysial cells (Tfap2b+; Aldh1a2+) was relatively low (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-expression analysis in UMAP plots showing Twist1 expression pattern (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claims.claim: At E13.5, Twist1 is expressed at a low level in the palate primordium and perimysial sites in the LVP region.
claims.source: In the LVP region, at E13.5 Twist1 was expressed at a low level in the palate primordium and perimysial sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing low Twist1 expression at E13.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C).

claims.claim: At E14.5, expression of Twist1 in the palate primordium had increased, whereas its expression was maintained at a low level in the perimysial site.
claims.source: At E14.5, expression of Twist1 in the palate primordium had increased, whereas its expression was maintained at a low level in the perimysial site (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing increased Twist1 expression in the palate primordium but low expression in the perimysial site at E14.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-E).

claims.claim: At E15.5, Twist1 showed a similar expression pattern to that of E14.5.
claims.source: At E15.5, Twist1 showed a similar expression pattern to that of E14.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing similar Twist1 expression pattern at E15.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F-G).

claims.claim: The spatiotemporally specific Twist1 expression in the palate primordium and myogenic regions of the soft palate is accompanied by an opposite trend in Runx2 expression in the same regions at the same stages.
claims.source: This spatiotemporally specific Twist1 expression in the palate primordium and myogenic regions of the soft palate was accompanied by an opposite trend in Runx2 expression in the same regions at the same stages.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Twist1 and Runx2 expression patterns across developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-G, Figure 2K-M).

claims.claim: Expression levels of Runx2 and Twist1 are tightly coordinated during soft palate development.
claims.source: This spatiotemporally specific Twist1 expression in the palate primordium and myogenic regions of the soft palate was accompanied by an opposite trend in Runx2 expression in the same regions at the same stages. This is perhaps shown most clearly by the colocalization of Runx2 and Twist1 in the LVP region at E14.5 (Figure 5D–G), which suggested that expression levels of Runx2 and Twist1 are tightly coordinated during soft palate development.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the complementary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 (Figure 5D-G).

claims.claim: Expression of Twist1 is upregulated in most of the palatal shelf region including the perimysial cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, we discovered that expression of Twist1 was upregulated in most of the palatal shelf region including the perimysial cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5H–K), which suggests that upregulation of Twist1 in the CNC-derived cells may interrupt their fate determination.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing increased Twist1 expression in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5H-K).

claims.claim: Upregulation of Twist1 in the CNC-derived cells may interrupt their fate determination.
claims.source: Interestingly, we discovered that expression of Twist1 was upregulated in most of the palatal shelf region including the perimysial cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5H–K), which suggests that upregulation of Twist1 in the CNC-derived cells may interrupt their fate determination.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of Twist1 in Runx2 mutants and the altered cell fate composition (Figure 5H-K, Figure 5A-B).

claims.claim: Both Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites are present in the regulatory region located around 15–40 kb downstream of the genetic locus of perimysial marker Aldh1a2.
claims.source: Based on the complimentary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 in the soft palate, we hypothesized that they may oppose each other in regulating their common downstream targets which are important for fate determination of CNC-derived cells. Therefore, we performed ATAC-seq and found that both Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites are present in the regulatory region located around 15–40 kb downstream of the genetic locus of perimysial marker Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A), suggesting that both Runx2 and Twist1 might directly regulate the expression of Aldh1a2.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis showing Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites near Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: Both Runx2 and Twist1 might directly regulate the expression of Aldh1a2.
claims.source: Based on the complimentary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 in the soft palate, we hypothesized that they may oppose each other in regulating their common downstream targets which are important for fate determination of CNC-derived cells. Therefore, we performed ATAC-seq and found that both Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites are present in the regulatory region located around 15–40 kb downstream of the genetic locus of perimysial marker Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A), suggesting that both Runx2 and Twist1 might directly regulate the expression of Aldh1a2.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites in the regulatory region of Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: Runx2 and Twist1 are likely to regulate Aldh1a2 independently because their binding sites are more than 20 kb apart.
claims.source: However, as the binding sites of those two transcription factors are more than 20 kb apart, they are likely to regulate Aldh1a2 independently.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the distance between Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites in the Aldh1a2 regulatory region (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: None of the five newborn Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ pups had palatal clefts, compared to the 50% penetrance of cleft soft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
claims.source: Histological analysis confirmed that the palatal stromal mesenchyme, pterygoid plate, and muscle defects were all indeed rescued in these mice. None of the five newborn Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ pups we collected had palatal clefts, compared to the 50% penetrance of cleft soft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6B–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing no cleft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B-G).

claims.claim: Pterygoid plate height was restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
claims.source: Pterygoid plate height was restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B–D,H), and muscle fiber orientation and muscle size were also recovered (Figure 6E–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis and quantification showing restored pterygoid plate height (Figure 6B-D, H).

claims.claim: Muscle fiber orientation and muscle size were recovered in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
claims.source: Pterygoid plate height was restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B–D,H), and muscle fiber orientation and muscle size were also recovered (Figure 6E–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing recovered muscle fiber orientation and size (Figure 6E-G).

claims.claim: Aldh1a2 was downregulated in the region where Runx2 was deleted in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E14.5.
claims.source: Aldh1a2 was downregulated in the region (Figure 6K) where Runx2 was deleted (Figure 6N) and Twist1 expression was expanded in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6Q).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing reduced Aldh1a2 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 6K).

claims.claim: Twist1 expression was expanded in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E14.5.
claims.source: Aldh1a2 was downregulated in the region (Figure 6K) where Runx2 was deleted (Figure 6N) and Twist1 expression was expanded in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6Q).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing expanded Twist1 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 6Q).

claims.claim: The expression of Aldh1a2 was restored in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice at E14.5.
claims.source: Compared to Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, the expression of Aldh1a2 was restored in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+mice at E14.5 (Figure 6L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing restored Aldh1a2 expression in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6L).

claims.claim: Runx2 and Twist1 exhibit opposite regulatory effects on the expression of Aldh1a2 in a subset of CNC-derived cells, which may be important for regulating muscle differentiation in the soft palate.
claims.source: Compared to Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, the expression of Aldh1a2 was restored in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+mice at E14.5 (Figure 6L). This suggests that Runx2 and Twist1 exhibit opposite regulatory effects on the expression of Aldh1a2 in a subset of CNC-derived cells, which may be important for regulating muscle differentiation in the soft palate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of Aldh1a2 expression and muscle defects by Twist1 haploinsufficiency (Figure 6L, Figure 6B-G).

claims.claim: Runx2 activates the expression of Aldh1a2 through repressing Twist1 instead of directly activating Aldh1a2 during normal soft palate muscle development.
claims.source: Since haploinsufficiency of Twist1 in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice rescues the expression of Aldh1a, it is most likely that Runx2 activates the expression of Aldh1a2 through repressing Twist1 instead of directly activating Aldh1a2 during normal soft palate muscle development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic rescue experiment showing that reducing Twist1 levels restores Aldh1a2 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 6L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Aldh1a2 is an important enzyme for retinoic acid signaling, which is crucial for neural crest cells as they guide the positioning of extraocular muscles.
claims.source: Consistent with our findings, Aldh1a2 is known as an important enzyme for retinoic acid signaling, which is crucial for neural crest cells as they guide the positioning of extraocular muscles (Matt et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies showing the role of Aldh1a2 in retinoic acid signaling and muscle development (Matt et al., 2008).

claims.claim: The Hic1+ population represents a source of quiescent mesenchymal progenitors that play important roles during the regeneration of skeletal muscles in the limbs.
claims.source: The potential myogenic-supportive function of Hic1 has been confirmed by the recent finding that the Hic1+ population represents a source of quiescent mesenchymal progenitors that play important roles during the regeneration of skeletal muscles in the limbs (Scott et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on a recent study showing the role of Hic1+ cells in muscle regeneration (Scott et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Aldh1a2 and Hic1 might be novel markers for CNC-derived perimysial tissues, which may perform important pro-myogenic functions during muscle development.
claims.source: Consistent with our findings, Aldh1a2 is known as an important enzyme for retinoic acid signaling, which is crucial for neural crest cells as they guide the positioning of extraocular muscles (Matt et al., 2008). The potential myogenic-supportive function of Hic1 has been confirmed by the recent finding that the Hic1+ population represents a source of quiescent mesenchymal progenitors that play important roles during the regeneration of skeletal muscles in the limbs (Scott et al., 2019). Hence, Aldh1a2 and Hic1 might be novel markers for CNC-derived perimysial tissues, which may perform important pro-myogenic functions during muscle development.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Aldh1a2 and Hic1 in perimysial tissues and their known roles in muscle development (Matt et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The least differentiated Tfap2b+ subpopulation is located in the lateral region of the soft palate during the early stages of its development.
claims.source: During embryonic development, the palatal shelves grow in a lateral-to-medial direction both before and after their elevation (Bush and Jiang, 2012). Consistent with this, our in vivo analysis shows that the least differentiated Tfap2b+ subpopulation is located in the lateral region of the soft palate during the early stages of its development, and the perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations reside in central myogenic sites and the medial region of the soft palate.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Tfap2b expression in the lateral region (Figure 1G).

claims.claim: The perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations reside in central myogenic sites and the medial region of the soft palate.
claims.source: During embryonic development, the palatal shelves grow in a lateral-to-medial direction both before and after their elevation (Bush and Jiang, 2012). Consistent with this, our in vivo analysis shows that the least differentiated Tfap2b+ subpopulation is located in the lateral region of the soft palate during the early stages of its development, and the perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations reside in central myogenic sites and the medial region of the soft palate.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing perimysial markers in central myogenic sites and Tbx22 in the medial region (Figure 1H-K).

claims.claim: Several transcription factors regulate the development of different components of a musculoskeletal complex in a coordinated fashion to form a functional unit.
claims.source: Recently, studies have found that several transcription factors regulate the development of different components of a musculoskeletal complex in a coordinated fashion to form a functional unit (Colasanto et al., 2016; Hasson et al., 2010; Mathew et al., 2011; Vickerman et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies showing coordinated regulation of musculoskeletal development (Colasanto et al., 2016; Hasson et al., 2010; Mathew et al., 2011; Vickerman et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells of the soft palate mesenchyme leads to multiple tissue defects in the soft palate, including fibrous tendon tissue, soft palate cleft and muscle defects.
claims.source: Our study shows that Runx2 is expressed in CNC-derived cells involved in early cell fate determination and in perimysial cells in the soft palate mesenchyme. Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells of the soft palate mesenchyme leads to multiple tissue defects in the soft palate, including fibrous tendon tissue, soft palate cleft and muscle defects.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis and CT scans showing multiple tissue defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3).

claims.claim: There is a fate change of CNC-derived cells from perimysial cells to midline mesenchymal cells in the soft palate of Runx2 mutant mice.
claims.source: There is a fate change of CNC-derived cells from perimysial cells to midline mesenchymal cells in the soft palate of Runx2 mutant mice.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by single-cell RNA-seq analysis showing altered cell cluster composition in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5A-B).

claims.claim: Loss of Runx2 affecting perimysial cell differentiation may in turn affect their secretion of signaling cues that promote muscle proliferation and differentiation.
claims.source: As perimysial cells are closely associated with muscle development, loss of Runx2 affecting their differentiation may in turn affect their secretion of signaling cues that promote muscle proliferation and differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the altered perimysial cell fate and the known role of perimysial cells in muscle development.

claims.claim: Multiple genes associated with pro-myogenic secreted factors specifically expressed by perimysial populations, such as Aldh1a2, Igf1, Cxcl12, and Cthrc1, are downregulated in Runx2 mutant mice.
claims.source: Indeed, we show that multiple genes associated with pro-myogenic secreted factors specifically expressed by perimysial populations, such as Aldh1a2, Igf1, Cxcl12, and Cthrc1, are downregulated in Runx2 mutant mice (Matt et al., 2008; Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011; Spector et al., 2013; Vasyutina et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq analysis showing downregulation of these genes in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claims.claim: Runx2 regulates the differentiation of CNC-derived cells during early tooth and intramembranous bone formation through distinct sets of downstream targets.
claims.source: Transcription factors often regulate different downstream targets in distinct tissues. Previous studies have shown that Runx2 regulates the differentiation of CNC-derived cells during early tooth and intramembranous bone formation through distinct sets of downstream targets including Gli1, Lef1, Tcf1, Wnt10a, Wnt10b, and Tgfb1 in osteogenic cells and Dusp6, Enpp1, Igfbp3, and Fgf3 in dental mesenchyme (James et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies showing tissue-specific Runx2 targets (James et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue.
claims.source: In this study, we have shown that downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue. Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2, while genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq and in situ hybridization showing differential gene expression changes in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2.
claims.source: In this study, we have shown that downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue. Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2, while genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization showing reduced expression of Aldh1a2 and Hic1 in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-H).

claims.claim: Genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated upon loss of Runx2.
claims.source: In this study, we have shown that downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue. Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2, while genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq showing upregulation of midline mesenchymal markers and general markers in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claims.claim: Runx2's different regulatory effects on distinct downstream targets in the soft palate mesenchyme could be direct or indirect.
claims.source: Although Runx2 has both transcriptional activation and repression domains, its different regulatory effects on distinct downstream targets in the soft palate mesenchyme could be direct or indirect.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the known dual function of Runx2 as both activator and repressor.

claims.claim: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells leads to abnormal upregulation of Twist1 in the perimysial population.
claims.source: In this study, we reveal complimentary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 in the perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations during soft palate development, which seems to confirm their antagonistic interaction (Bialek et al., 2004). However, in contrast to the previously reported model of Twist1 and Runx2 antagonistic interaction, we show that loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells leads to abnormal upregulation of Twist1 in the perimysial population.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing increased Twist1 expression in the perimysial region of Runx2 mutants (Figure 5H-K).

claims.claim: Suppression of Twist1 in the perimysial population by Runx2 is necessary to maintain the expression level of perimysial marker gene Aldh1a2, which may be important for regulating muscle development.
claims.source: Further analysis has shown that suppression of Twist1 in the perimysial population by Runx2 is necessary to maintain the expression level of perimysial marker gene Aldh1a2, which may be important for regulating muscle development.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue of Aldh1a2 expression and muscle defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6J-L, Figure 6B-G).

claims.claim: The regulation of myogenesis by perimysial CNC-derived cells through Runx2-Twist1 interaction in the soft palate might also be shared by other craniofacial musculoskeletal structures.
claims.source: In summary, our study reveals a complex cellular heterogeneity within the developing soft palate and demonstrates that distinct subpopulations of CNC-derived cells are associated with distinct functions, which coordinate to form intricately connected components of the oropharyngeal complex. Moreover, the regulation of myogenesis by perimysial CNC-derived cells through Runx2-Twist1 interaction in the soft palate might also be shared by other craniofacial musculoskeletal structures.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression of perimysial markers in multiple craniofacial muscle regions (Figure 1P-R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E).

results.result: CNC cells give rise to craniofacial skeletal tissues and regulate muscle development through cell-cell interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-established facts in the field, supported by multiple citations to prior work (Chai and Maxson, 2006; Heude et al., 2010; Le Douarin et al., 2004; Grimaldi et al., 2015; Han et al., 2014; Rinon et al., 2007). These are foundational background claims that provide context for the study.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq identified 8 cell types and revealed heterogeneity within CNC-derived mesenchymal cells, including progenitors, midline mesenchymal cells, perimysial cells, and mitotic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C14 are supported by single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 1A-B) showing distinct clusters with characteristic marker gene expression. The identification of cell types is based on known markers and functional annotation, with appropriate citations to support the functional interpretations.

results.result: In situ hybridization validated the spatial distribution of identified cell clusters in the developing soft palate.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C21 are supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data (Figure 1E-L, M-T) showing the anatomical localization of cluster-specific markers. The spatial patterns are consistent with the predicted cell identities from scRNA-seq analysis.

results.result: Perimysial markers are expressed in mesenchyme surrounding multiple craniofacial muscles, suggesting a common CNC-derived population involved in muscle development.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by in situ hybridization showing perimysial marker expression in tongue, masseter, and other craniofacial muscle regions (Figure 1P-R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E). The inference that this represents a common population is reasonable but would benefit from lineage tracing experiments.

results.result: Perimysial markers show differential expression in hard versus soft palate, with Tbx15 absent from hard palate while Aldh1a2 and Hic1 are expressed around tooth germs.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-F). The inference that these markers have different functions in hard versus soft palate (C26) is reasonable but speculative without functional validation.

results.result: Perimysial markers show temporal and spatial expression patterns in the tongue, with Aldh1a2 potentially associated with early myogenic populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are supported by in situ hybridization showing temporal changes in marker expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-F). The inferences about association with myogenic populations (C30-C31) are reasonable but speculative without functional validation.

results.result: CNC-derived cell heterogeneity decreases during development, with progenitor populations declining and differentiated populations increasing.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by temporal scRNA-seq analysis (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The inference that declining clusters represent transient progenitors (C36) is supported by pseudotime analysis but could benefit from lineage tracing validation.

results.result: Pseudotime analysis predicts that Cluster 0 represents common progenitors that bifurcate into perimysial and midline mesenchymal lineages at E13.5-E14.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by Monocle 3 pseudotime trajectory analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C). However, pseudotime analysis is computational inference and would benefit from experimental validation through lineage tracing.

results.result: Runx2 expression decreases during development and is predominantly expressed in progenitor and perimysial populations, with minimal expression in midline mesenchymal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by scRNA-seq data showing temporal and cluster-specific Runx2 expression patterns (Figure 2B, C-J). The inference about Runx2's role in differentiation (C41) is reasonable but requires functional validation.

results.result: Runx2 protein expression is spatially and temporally restricted during soft palate development, localizing to progenitor, perimysial, and osteogenic sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization data (Figure 2K-X) showing Runx2 expression patterns. The spatial restriction is well-documented across developmental stages.

results.result: Runx2 may regulate CNC-derived cell differentiation in a cell-autonomous manner, indirectly affecting myogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is a hypothesis inferred from Runx2 expression patterns and prior knowledge. While reasonable, this requires experimental validation through loss-of-function studies, which are presented later in the manuscript.

results.result: Osr2-Cre labels CNC-derived cells in the soft palate, including perimysial cells, and can be used to delete Runx2 in these populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by lineage tracing data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-G) showing tdTomato+ cells in soft palate mesenchyme and co-expression with Runx2. This validates the genetic strategy for conditional deletion.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells causes cleft soft palate (50% penetrance), muscle defects (100%), and skeletal defects with variable severity.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by phenotypic analysis of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3A-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J). The correlation between skeletal defect severity and cleft penetrance (C56) is based on limited sample size (N=6) but shows a clear trend.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 causes pterygoid plate defects, abnormal muscle attachment, and tendon defects in the TVP region.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by histological analysis and in situ hybridization (Figure 3G-H, L-M, Figure 3—figure supplement 3I-L, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-D). The inference that muscle attachment defects are due to hard tissue and aponeurosis disruption (C61) is reasonable given the lack of Runx2 expression in TVP perimysium.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 causes muscle defects in the LVP region, including reduced size, misoriented fibers, and centralized nuclei, indicating both direct and indirect effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by histological analysis (Figure 3I-P, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-D, G-H). The muscle fiber misorientation and centralized nuclei are well-documented. The conclusion about direct and indirect effects (C67) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Muscle defects in Runx2 mutants appear at E14.5, with delayed differentiation evidenced by reduced MHC expression and presence of immature myoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 are supported by temporal analysis of myogenic markers (Figure 4A-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D). The inference about delayed differentiation (C71) is reasonable based on reduced late marker expression. The speculation about functional consequences (C74) is not directly tested.

results.result: CNC-derived cell proliferation is normal in Runx2 mutants, but myogenic cell proliferation is reduced at E15.5, with no change in apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by BrdU incorporation and caspase3 staining (Figure 4E-L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H). Statistical analysis shows significant reduction in myogenic proliferation at E15.5 (p=0.02). The inference about altered signaling (C79) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 alters CNC-derived cell composition, with decreased perimysial cells and increased midline mesenchymal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by integration analysis of E14.5 scRNA-seq data (Figure 5A-B). The altered cell composition suggests a fate switch, though the analysis is descriptive and would benefit from quantitative statistical testing of cluster proportions.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 reduces expression of perimysial markers and causes differential expression of CNC-derived cell-specific genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by in situ hybridization and bulk RNA-seq (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-I). The data show consistent downregulation of perimysial markers and upregulation of other genes. The inference about myogenic defects (C84) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Twist1 shows complementary expression to Runx2 during soft palate development, with high expression in midline mesenchyme and low expression in perimysial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 are supported by scRNA-seq and in situ hybridization data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-G, Figure 5D-G). The complementary expression patterns are well-documented. The inference about tight coordination (C93) is reasonable but descriptive.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 causes upregulation of Twist1 in perimysial cells, potentially disrupting cell fate determination.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by in situ hybridization showing expanded Twist1 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5H-K). The inference about fate determination (C95) is reasonable given the altered cell composition but requires further validation.

results.result: ATAC-seq reveals Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites near Aldh1a2, suggesting both factors may regulate its expression independently.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by ATAC-seq data (Figure 6A). The presence of binding sites suggests potential regulation, but the inference about independent regulation (C98) based on distance (>20 kb) is speculative without functional validation.

results.result: Twist1 haploinsufficiency rescues soft palate defects in Runx2 mutants, including cleft palate, pterygoid plate height, and muscle defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by histological analysis of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B-H). The complete rescue of cleft palate (0/5 vs 5/10) and restoration of muscle and skeletal phenotypes provide strong evidence for genetic interaction. However, sample size is limited (N=5).

results.result: Runx2 maintains Aldh1a2 expression by suppressing Twist1, as evidenced by rescue of Aldh1a2 expression in Twist1 haploinsufficient Runx2 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 are supported by in situ hybridization showing downregulation of Aldh1a2 and upregulation of Twist1 in Runx2 mutants, with restoration in double mutants (Figure 6J-R). The genetic epistasis experiment provides strong evidence for the proposed regulatory mechanism (C106).

results.result: Aldh1a2 and Hic1 are novel markers for CNC-derived perimysial tissues with pro-myogenic functions, based on their known roles in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by citations to prior work showing roles of Aldh1a2 in extraocular muscle development (Matt et al., 2008) and Hic1 in muscle regeneration (Scott et al., 2019). The inference that these are novel perimysial markers (C109) is reasonable but requires functional validation in the soft palate context.

results.result: The spatial distribution of CNC-derived cell types follows the lateral-to-medial growth pattern of palatal shelves.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1G-K) and are consistent with known palatal shelf growth patterns (Bush and Jiang, 2012). This provides anatomical context for the differentiation hierarchy.

results.result: Runx2 coordinates development of multiple soft palate tissues by regulating CNC-derived cell fate, with loss causing fate changes and reduced expression of pro-myogenic factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 are supported by the combined evidence from scRNA-seq, phenotypic analysis, and bulk RNA-seq. The coordinated regulation of multiple tissues (C112) is supported by prior work. The fate change (C114) and downregulation of pro-myogenic factors (C116) are well-documented.

results.result: Runx2 regulates different downstream targets in different tissues, with tissue-specific responses to Runx2 loss in soft palate.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 are supported by comparison to prior work (James et al., 2006) and bulk RNA-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I). The differential responses of perimysial versus midline markers are well-documented. The speculation about direct versus indirect effects (C121) is reasonable.

results.result: Loss of Runx2 causes abnormal upregulation of Twist1 in perimysial cells, and suppression of Twist1 by Runx2 is necessary to maintain Aldh1a2 expression and muscle development.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 are supported by the genetic rescue experiment showing restoration of Aldh1a2 expression and muscle phenotypes in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6). This provides strong evidence for the proposed regulatory mechanism.

results.result: The Runx2-Twist1 regulatory mechanism in soft palate perimysial cells may be shared by other craniofacial musculoskeletal structures.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is inferred from the widespread expression of perimysial markers in multiple craniofacial muscles (Figure 1P-R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E). While reasonable, this hypothesis requires functional validation in other craniofacial muscle systems.
